0Two alphabets, one set of sounds

Japanese has two sound alphabets that say exactly the same sounds. Hiragana is curvy and writes ordinary Japanese words and grammar. Katakana is angular and writes words borrowed from other languages, foreign names, and signs that want to stand out. Learn the sounds once and you can sound out both.

Signs and menus also use kanji, the Chinese characters, which carry meaning and have to be learned one by one. They are not covered here.

1Five vowels that never change

Every sound in Japanese ends in one of these five vowels (or is ん). Unlike English, each vowel is always said the same way, short and clean. Get these right and most of the rest is a consonant plus one of them.

Watch out for these

  • Say “she”, never “see”.

  • Say “chee” as in cheese, never “tee”.

  • The ts at the end of “cats”, then oo. Start the word with it: “tsoo”.

  • Softer than an English f. Blow gently through rounded lips, like cooling soup. Your top teeth don’t touch your lip.

  • The whole r row is one quick tap of the tongue just behind the top teeth, like the dd in “ladder” said fast. It sits between r, l and d. Never roll it or growl it.

  • A breathier h than usual, close to the start of “huge”.

  • Sounds exactly like お. It is only ever used as a grammar word.

  • Hums through the nose for one full beat. It turns into m before p, b or m (さんぽ is “sampo”).

3Two dots and a small circle

Two little dots (゛) on the top right make the sound buzzier: k becomes g, s becomes z, t becomes d, and h becomes b. A small circle (゜) only goes on the h row and turns it into p. The g is always hard, as in “go”, never as in “gem”.

ぢ and づ sound the same as じ and ず and are rare. You will almost always see じ and ず.

4Blends with a small ゃ ゅ ょ

A character from the i column followed by a small や, ゆ or よ squeezes the two into one beat: き plus a small ゃ is “kya”, one sound, not “ki-ya”. Size matters here, and so does the beat count.

yayuyokstnhmrgjbp

5Rhythm: the rules that change words

Japanese words are counted in beats, one per kana, and every beat is about the same length. Each box below is one beat, and a faded letter is whispered. Getting the beat count wrong is the most common way to say a different word by accident.

Every kana is one beat

Japanese is timed like a metronome. Each kana gets the same short beat, and no syllable is stressed louder than the others. English speakers tend to say “to-KYO”; Japanese is four even beats.

Long vowels take two beats

A vowel held twice as long is a different word. In hiragana the vowel is written twice (おう and えい usually just stretch the o and the e). In katakana a dash ー stretches the sound before it.

A small っ is a pause

A small っ (ッ in katakana) has no sound of its own. It is a one-beat pause where your mouth is ready for the next consonant, like the catch in “bookcase” or “hot tea”.

ん gets its own beat

ん is a full beat even though it is only an n. Don’t swallow it into the next sound.

Some u and i sounds are whispered

Between sounds like k, s, t, h and p, and at the end of です and ます, the u and i are almost silent. すき sounds like “ski”.

Three grammar words break the rules

When they are used as grammar words, は is said wa, へ is said e, and を is said o. Everywhere else they keep their chart sound.

Japanese words also rise and fall a little in pitch instead of stressing one syllable louder. Beginners can ignore pitch and still be understood; even beats matter much more.

6Extra katakana for foreign sounds

Katakana adds a small vowel to make sounds Japanese doesn’t have, so borrowed words come out closer to the original.

Why English words sound different in Japanese

Every consonant in Japanese needs a vowel after it (only ん stands alone), so borrowed words gain extra beats. Knowing this makes katakana menus easy to sound out.

7Easy to mix up

  • シ: the two short strokes sit on the left and the long one sweeps up from the bottom. ツ: the short strokes sit along the top and the long one falls down from the top.

  • Same idea with one short stroke. ン sweeps up from the bottom; ソ falls from the top.

  • ぬ ends in a small loop; め doesn’t.

  • Same left side. ね ends in a loop, れ kicks out to the right, わ curls back round.

  • る has a loop at the bottom; ろ is open.

  • Mirror images. The bottom of さ bulges left, like a c; the bottom of ち bulges right, like the bottom of a 5.

  • ほ has an extra line across the top.

  • These look almost the same in both scripts, and they sound the same too.
